note: Notes that 81 percent of trials report positive endpoints while mostly single centre, which is a publication bias warning an audit should carry.
title: Randomised controlled trials evaluating artificial intelligence in clinical practice: a scoping review

reading.body:
Eighty-one percent of randomised trials of AI in clinical practice report positive results, and most were run at a single centre, which is a publication bias warning rather than a sign of maturity.

The pattern is narrow and favourable. Of 86 trials, 70 reported positive main outcomes, concentrated in deep learning for medical imaging, especially gastroenterology and radiology, with the United States and China running the most. A field where four in five attempts succeed is not a field that has been tested hard. Single-centre design compounds this: results from one hospital's scanners, staff, and patient mix do not transfer automatically to another's.

For AI specifically, the gap between a positive endpoint and a deployable system runs through infrastructure. Trials that measure how well a model finds disease say little about whether it holds up across sites, whether it fits clinical workflow, or what compute and data pipelines it needs to run continuously. The review notes that efficiency results varied and that patient demographics were rarely described, so the operational and equity questions are largely unanswered.

What this does not cover: it is a scoping review of trial design and reporting, not a measure of clinical benefit, cost, or power demand. It counts trials and their stated outcomes. It cannot say whether the positive results are real, only that their concentration and their single-centre setting make them less certain than the headline number suggests.

explain_beginner: This review looked at randomised trials that studied artificial intelligence in real clinical care. It found growing interest worldwide, with the United States and China running the most trials. Most work used deep learning for medical images, especially in gastroenterology and radiology. Of 86 trials, 70 reported positive main results, often about finding disease or test performance. But many were done at one centre, few described patient demographics, and efficiency results varied. That makes the findings less certain for wider use. The authors warn that positive results may be overrepresented and call for broader, patient-focused research.
explain_business: This review suggests AI in clinical care is attracting growing study, especially in the USA and China and in medical imaging for gastroenterology and radiology. Most of the 86 randomised trials reported positive main results, often around finding disease or test performance. But many were run at a single site, patient demographics were rarely described, and efficiency results were inconsistent. So the evidence is promising but not yet broad enough for confident deployment. Executives should treat these results as early signals, not proof. Decisions should favour multicentre validation, clear reporting, workflow testing, and outcomes that matter to patients before scaling AI.
explain_practitioner: This scoping review mapped randomised controlled trials of AI in clinical practice. The authors found 86 trials and examined specialties, locations, AI methods, and results. Interest is expanding. The USA and China contribute the most trials. Deep learning for medical imaging dominates, especially gastroenterology and radiology. Seventy trials, 81 percent, reported positive main outcomes, mostly about how well tests found disease or performed. However, most were single-centre, demographic reporting was limited, and workflow efficiency findings varied. These factors limit generalisability and practicality. The review highlights likely publication bias and recommends multicentre trials, broader measures, better reporting, and outcomes that matter to patients to clarify AI's real effects and limits.
